title: Οὐλὴ καὶ τόξον
titleEn: The Scar and the Request for the Bow — Odyssey 21.207–319
part: The Scar and the Request for the Bow (21.207–319)
about: Odysseus speaks to the cowherd and the swineherd. He says that no other servant prayed for his return, and promises them wives, houses and the standing of Telemachus’ brothers if a god lets him overcome the suitors. As a plain sign he shows them the scar from the boar on Parnassus, and they weep and embrace him until he stops them and gives his orders: the men are to go in one by one, Eumaeus is to bring him the bow, the women are to be shut in, and Philoetius is to bolt the courtyard gates. Inside, Eurymachus cannot string the bow, even warming it at the fire, and laments the shame. Antinous proposes to put the contest off until the next day, the god’s festival. Odysseus asks to try the bow himself. The suitors take offence, and Antinous rebukes him with the tale of the Centaur ruined by wine and threatens to send him to King Echetus. Penelope protests that Telemachus’ guests must not be wronged.

sentences.t:
ἔνδον μὲν δὴ ὅδ’ αὐτὸς ἐγώ, κακὰ πολλὰ μογήσας
ἤλυθον εἰκοστῷ ἔτεϊ ἐς πατρίδα γαῖαν.
sentences.l:
“Within, indeed, here am I myself, having toiled through many evils,
I have come in the twentieth year to my fatherland.
sentences.i: “Here I am, indoors, I myself, after toiling through many evils; I have come in the twentieth year to my fatherland.
sentences.n: ὅδ’ αὐτὸς ἐγώ is ‘here am I myself’: ὅδε points at the speaker, and ἔνδον ‘within’ puts him in the house, so the stranger names himself in his first words. μογήσας is the aorist participle of μογέω ‘toil, suffer hardship’, with κακὰ πολλά as its object. ἤλυθον is the epic form of Attic ἦλθον. εἰκοστῷ ἔτεϊ is a dative of time, ‘in the twentieth year’. The second line repeats one already shipped and keeps its wording.

sentences.t:
γιγνώσκω δ’ ὡς σφῶϊν ἐελδομένοισιν ἱκάνω
οἴοισι δμώων·
sentences.l:
And I know that to you two, longing for me, I have come,
alone of the servants;
sentences.i: I know that I have come to two who long for me, you alone of the servants;
sentences.n: σφῶϊν is the dual ‘to you two’, the cowherd and the swineherd, and ἐελδομένοισιν ‘longing’, from ἔλδομαι, agrees with it although the participle has a plural ending. ὡς after γιγνώσκω is ‘that’, and ἱκάνω is ‘I have come, I arrive’. οἴοισι δμώων is ‘alone of the servants’, οἶος ‘alone’ with a partitive genitive. The raised dot after δμώων ends the unit in the middle of line 210.

sentences.t:
τῶν δ’ ἄλλων οὔ τευ ἄκουσα
εὐξαμένου ἐμὲ αὖτις ὑπότροπον οἴκαδ’ ἱκέσθαι.
sentences.l:
but of the others not one did I hear
praying that I again, returned, should come home.
sentences.i: but of the others I have heard none pray that I might return home again.
sentences.n: τῶν δ’ ἄλλων is ‘but of the others’, and τευ is τινός ‘anyone’. The genitive εὐξαμένου, the aorist participle of εὔχομαι ‘pray’, is the object of ἄκουσα ‘I heard’, which has no augment: ‘I heard no one praying’. ὑπότροπον ‘turned back, returning’ agrees with ἐμέ, and ἱκέσθαι is the aorist infinitive of ἱκνέομαι ‘come’, in indirect speech after εὐξαμένου. οἴκαδ’ is οἴκαδε ‘homeward’.

sentences.t: σφῶϊν δ’, ὡς ἔσεταί περ, ἀληθείην καταλέξω.
sentences.l: And to you two, just as it will be, the truth I will recount.
sentences.i: To you two I will recount the truth, just as it shall be.
sentences.n: ἔσεταί is the future of εἰμί in its epic form with one σ (Attic ἔσται), and περ adds ‘precisely’ to ὡς: ‘just as it will be’. What is to come is the matter of the next lines. ἀληθείην is the Ionic form of ἀλήθειαν ‘truth’, and καταλέξω the future of καταλέγω ‘recount in full’. σφῶϊν is the dual ‘to you two’ again.

sentences.t:
εἴ χ’ ὑπ’ ἐμοί γε θεὸς δαμάσῃ μνηστῆρας ἀγαυούς,
ἄξομαι ἀμφοτέροις ἀλόχους καὶ κτήματ’ ὀπάσσω
οἰκία τ’ ἐγγὺς ἐμεῖο τετυγμένα·
sentences.i: If a god overcomes the noble suitors at my hands, I will bring wives for you both, and give you possessions, and houses built near mine;
sentences.n: εἴ χ’ is εἰ κε, and with the aorist subjunctive δαμάσῃ it makes a condition that looks forward, ‘if a god subdues’. ὑπ’ ἐμοί ‘under me’ puts the suitors under Odysseus’ hand, so the god acts through him. ἄξομαι is the future middle of ἄγω, here ‘I will bring’, ἀμφοτέροις is ‘for both’, and κτήματ’ ὀπάσσω is ‘I will give possessions’, from ὀπάζω. μνηστῆρες ἀγαυοί ‘noble suitors’ is translated every time. The first line repeats one already shipped.

sentences.t:
καί μοι ἔπειτα
Τηλεμάχου ἑτάρω τε κασιγνήτω τε ἔσεσθον.
sentences.l:
and to me then
of Telemachus companions and brothers you two shall be.
sentences.i: and from then on you two shall be to me the companions and brothers of Telemachus.
sentences.n: ἑτάρω and κασιγνήτω are dual nominatives, ‘two companions’ and ‘two brothers’, and ἔσεσθον is the dual future of εἰμί, ‘you two will be’, so he is still speaking to both men. Τηλεμάχου is a genitive of relation, ‘of Telemachus’, and μοι ‘to me’ makes the bond personal. ἔπειτα ‘then, thereafter’ dates it from the victory. ἑτάρος is the epic form of ἑταῖρος.

sentences.t:
εἰ δ’ ἄγε δή, καὶ σῆμα ἀριφραδὲς ἄλλο τι δείξω,
ὄφρα μ’ ἐῢ γνῶτον πιστωθῆτόν τ’ ἐνὶ θυμῷ,
οὐλήν, τήν ποτέ με σῦς ἤλασε λευκῷ ὀδόντι
Παρνησόνδ’ ἐλθόντα σὺν υἱάσιν Αὐτολύκοιο.
sentences.l:
But come now, also a very plain sign, another, will I show,
so that you two may know me well and be convinced in your heart,
the scar, which once me a boar struck with a white tooth,
having gone to Parnassus with the sons of Autolycus.”
sentences.i: But come, I will show you another sign as well, a very plain one, so that you two may know me well and be convinced in your hearts: the scar that a boar once struck into me with its white tusk, when I had gone to Parnassus with the sons of Autolycus.”
sentences.n: εἰ δ’ ἄγε δή is a stock call to action, ‘come now’, and δείξω is a short-vowel aorist subjunctive, ‘let me show’. ἀριφραδές ‘very plain’ qualifies σῆμα. γνῶτον and πιστωθῆτον are dual subjunctives after ὄφρα, ‘that you two may know’ and ‘may be convinced’, the second the passive of πιστόω ‘make trustworthy’. οὐλήν ‘scar’ is in apposition to σῆμα. ἐλθόντα agrees with με, and Παρνησόνδ’ is ‘to Parnassus’ with the suffix -δε. The last line repeats one already shipped. This ends his speech.

sentences.t: ὣς εἰπὼν ῥάκεα μεγάλης ἀποέργαθεν οὐλῆς.
sentences.l: So having spoken, the rags from the great scar he pushed away.
sentences.i: So he spoke, and pushed the rags away from the great scar.
sentences.n: ὣς εἰπών ‘so having spoken’ is the usual way of closing a speech. ἀποέργαθεν is the aorist of ἀποέργω (Attic ἀπείργω ‘keep away, shut off’), an old form without augment, and μεγάλης οὐλῆς is a genitive of separation: the rags are moved off the scar. ῥάκεα ‘rags’ are the stranger’s torn clothes.

sentences.t:
τὼ δ’ ἐπεὶ εἰσιδέτην εὖ τ’ ἐφράσσαντο ἕκαστα,
κλαῖον ἄρ’ ἀμφ’ Ὀδυσῆϊ δαΐφρονι χεῖρε βαλόντε,
καὶ κύνεον ἀγαπαζόμενοι κεφαλήν τε καὶ ὤμους
ὣς δ’ αὔτως Ὀδυσεὺς κεφαλὰς καὶ χεῖρας ἔκυσσε.
sentences.l:
And the two, when they had looked and well marked each thing,
wept then, round Odysseus the wise-minded their arms throwing,
and kissed him, gladly welcoming, both head and shoulders,
and in the same way Odysseus kissed their heads and hands.
sentences.i: When the two had seen it and marked every detail well, they wept, throwing their arms round Odysseus the wise-hearted, and kissed his head and shoulders, welcoming him gladly; and Odysseus, in the same way, kissed their heads and hands.
sentences.n: The dual runs through the first lines: τὼ ‘the two’, εἰσιδέτην, and βαλόντε with χεῖρε ‘two arms’. ἐφράσσαντο is the aorist middle of φράζω ‘observe, mark’, and ἕκαστα ‘each thing’. ἀμφὶ … βαλόντε ‘throwing about’ is tmesis. The source prints no stop after ὤμους, so the sentence runs four lines. δαΐφρων is translated every time; its sense is doubtful (‘warlike’ or ‘wise’), and ‘wise’ is followed.

sentences.t:
καί νύ κ’ ὀδυρομένοισιν ἔδυ φάος ἠελίοιο,
εἰ μὴ Ὀδυσσεὺς αὐτὸς ἐρύκακε φώνησέν τε·
sentences.l:
And indeed, as they lamented, would have set the light of the sun,
if Odysseus himself had not held them back and spoken:
sentences.i: And the light of the sun would have gone down on them as they wept, if Odysseus himself had not held them back and spoken:
sentences.n: καί νύ κε with the aorist ἔδυ ‘set’ is the apodosis of a condition contrary to fact, ‘it would have set’, and εἰ μὴ … ἐρύκακε is its condition, ‘if he had not held them back’. ὀδυρομένοισιν is a dative plural participle, ‘as they lamented’. ἐρύκακε is a reduplicated aorist of ἐρύκω ‘restrain’. φώνησε is the aorist of φωνέω ‘speak’. The first line repeats one already shipped.

sentences.t:
παύεσθον κλαυθμοῖο γόοιό τε, μή τις ἴδηται
ἐξελθὼν μεγάροιο, ἀτὰρ εἴπῃσι καὶ εἴσω.
sentences.l:
“Cease, you two, from weeping and from wailing, lest anyone see,
coming out of the hall, and tell it also within.
sentences.i: “Stop your weeping and wailing, you two, in case anyone comes out of the hall, sees you, and tells it indoors as well.
sentences.n: παύεσθον is the dual imperative of παύομαι ‘cease’, with the genitives κλαυθμοῖο γόοιό τε ‘from weeping and wailing’. μή with the aorist subjunctive ἴδηται is ‘lest anyone see’, with the object left out. ἐξελθὼν μεγάροιο is ‘coming out of the hall’, a genitive of separation. εἴπῃσι is the subjunctive of εἶπον with the epic ending -σι, so ‘and tell’, and εἴσω ‘within’ is where the news would go.

sentences.t:
ἀλλὰ προμνηστῖνοι ἐσέλθετε, μηδ’ ἅμα πάντες,
πρῶτος ἐγώ, μετὰ δ’ ὔμμες·
sentences.l:
But one by one go in, and not all together,
I first, and after me you;
sentences.i: But go in one after another, not all at once: I first, and you after me;
sentences.n: προμνηστῖνοι is a rare word whose derivation is not known; the context, with μηδ’ ἅμα πάντες ‘nor all together’, gives ‘one after another’. ἐσέλθετε is the imperative of εἰσέρχομαι, with ἐς- for Attic εἰς-. πρῶτος ἐγώ ‘I first’ has no verb, and ὔμμες is an epic form of ὑμεῖς ‘you’, with μετά as the adverb ‘after’.

sentences.t: ἀτὰρ τόδε σῆμα τετύχθω·
sentences.l: but let this sign be made:
sentences.i: and let this be the sign:
sentences.n: τετύχθω is the perfect passive imperative, third person, of τεύχω ‘make’: ‘let it be made, let it stand’. ἀτάρ is ‘but, and now’, turning to a new point. σῆμα ‘sign’ was the scar in line 217; here it is a signal or arrangement, and the γάρ of the next line begins to explain it.

sentences.t:
ἄλλοι μὲν γὰρ πάντες, ὅσοι μνηστῆρες ἀγαυοί,
οὐκ ἐάσουσιν ἐμοὶ δόμεναι βιὸν ἠδὲ φαρέτρην·
sentences.l:
For the others, all, as many as are noble suitors,
will not allow to be given to me the bow and the quiver;
sentences.i: For all the others, as many as are noble suitors, will not let the bow and the quiver be given to me;
sentences.n: οὐκ ἐάσουσιν ἐμοὶ δόμεναι is ‘will not allow to be given to me’: ἐάσουσιν is the future of ἐάω, and δόμεναι is the infinitive of δίδωμι in the epic form in -μεναι (Attic δοῦναι). βιόν, accented on the last syllable, is ‘bow’, not βίος ‘life’. ὅσοι ‘as many as’ makes the suitors a body, and μνηστῆρες ἀγαυοί ‘noble suitors’ is translated every time. φαρέτρη is ‘quiver’.

sentences.t:
ἀλλὰ σύ, δῖ’ Εὔμαιε, φέρων ἀνὰ δώματα τόξον
ἐν χείρεσσιν ἐμοὶ θέμεναι, εἰπεῖν τε γυναιξὶ
κληῗσαι μεγάροιο θύρας πυκινῶς ἀραρυίας,
sentences.l:
But you, heavenly Eumaeus, carrying through the house the bow,
place it in my hands, and tell the women
to lock the doors of the hall, tightly fitted,
sentences.i: But you, heavenly Eumaeus, carry the bow through the house and put it in my hands, and tell the women to lock the tight-fitting doors of the hall,
sentences.n: θέμεναι, εἰπεῖν and κληῗσαι are infinitives used as commands, ‘put it … tell … lock’, which Homer allows where Attic would use the imperative; θέμεναι is the -μεναι form of θεῖναι. φέρων ἀνὰ δώματα is ‘carrying it through the house’. δῖ’ Εὔμαιε is a vocative, and δῖος is translated ‘heavenly’ every time. κληῗσαι ‘to lock, bar’ comes from κληΐς ‘bar, bolt, key’. ἀραρυίας is the feminine perfect participle of ἀραρίσκω ‘fit’, with πυκινῶς ‘closely’.

sentences.t:
ἢν δέ τις ἢ στοναχῆς ἠὲ κτύπου ἔνδον ἀκούσῃ
ἀνδρῶν ἡμετέροισιν ἐν ἕρκεσι, μή τι θύραζε
προβλώσκειν, ἀλλ’ αὐτοῦ ἀκὴν ἔμεναι παρὰ ἔργῳ.
sentences.l:
and if anyone either of groaning or of din within hears
of men in our courts, not at all out of doors
to go forth, but there in silence to stay beside their work.
sentences.i: and if any of them hears groaning or the din of men inside our courts, they are not to go out of doors at all, but to stay where they are, in silence, at their work.
sentences.n: ἢν δέ is ‘and if’ (ἐάν), and ἀκούσῃ takes the genitives στοναχῆς and κτύπου ‘groaning’ and ‘din’, with ἀνδρῶν ‘of men’ depending on both. μή τι … προβλώσκειν and ἔμεναι are again infinitives for commands, ‘not to go forth … but to stay’; ἔμεναι is the epic infinitive of εἰμί. θύραζε ‘out of doors’, αὐτοῦ ‘on the spot’ and ἀκήν ‘in silence’ are adverbs. ἕρκεσι is the dative plural of ἕρκος ‘court, enclosure’.

sentences.t:
σοὶ δέ, Φιλοίτιε δῖε, θύρας ἐπιτέλλομαι αὐλῆς
κληῗσαι κληῗδι, θοῶς δ’ ἐπὶ δεσμὸν ἰῆλαι.
sentences.l:
And to you, Philoetius, heavenly, I give charge, the doors of the courtyard
to lock with the bolt, and quickly to throw a rope on.”
sentences.i: And to you, heavenly Philoetius, I give the charge of locking the doors of the courtyard with the bolt, and quickly throwing a rope on.”
sentences.n: σοὶ δέ with the vocative Φιλοίτιε δῖε opens the order, and ἐπιτέλλομαι ‘I give charge’ takes the infinitive κληῗσαι ‘to lock’. κληΐς is whatever fastens a door, bar, bolt or key (it was a key in the storeroom scene); a bolt is likeliest here. ἐπὶ … ἰῆλαι is tmesis, the aorist infinitive of ἐπιάλλω ‘throw on’, and δεσμόν ‘bond’ is a rope or lashing. θοῶς is ‘quickly’. This ends Odysseus’ speech.

sentences.t: ὣς εἰπὼν εἰσῆλθε δόμους εὖ ναιετάοντας·
sentences.l: So having spoken, he entered the well-inhabited house;
sentences.i: So he spoke, and went into the well-inhabited house;
sentences.n: ὣς εἰπών is again ‘so having spoken’, and εἰσῆλθε the aorist ‘entered’. δόμους εὖ ναιετάοντας is a stock phrase, plural for one house, with ναιετάοντας the participle of ναιετάω ‘dwell’, so ‘well dwelt in’. The line repeats the first line of a unit already shipped.

sentences.t: ἕζετ’ ἔπειτ’ ἐπὶ δίφρον ἰών, ἔνθεν περ ἀνέστη·
sentences.l: He sat down then, going to the stool, from where he had risen;
sentences.i: Then he went to the stool he had risen from, and sat down;
sentences.n: ἕζετ’ is ἕζετο, ‘sat down’, without augment, and ἰών is the participle of εἶμι ‘go’. δίφρος is ‘stool’. ἔνθεν περ ἀνέστη is ‘from the very place he had risen’, with the suffix -θεν ‘from’ and περ sharpening it. Elsewhere the same words are said of a chair, θρόνος.

sentences.t: ἐς δ’ ἄρα καὶ τὼ δμῶε ἴτην θείου Ὀδυσῆος.
sentences.l: and in, then, also the two servants went, of divine Odysseus.
sentences.i: and the two servants of divine Odysseus went in as well.
sentences.n: ἴτην is the dual imperfect of εἶμι ‘go’, matching τὼ δμῶε ‘the two servants’, a dual of δμώς; they are the cowherd and the swineherd. ἐς … ἴτην is tmesis for ‘went in’. θείου ‘divine’ is the epithet used here of Odysseus; it is kept apart from δῖος ‘heavenly’ and translated every time.

sentences.t:
Εὐρύμαχος δ’ ἤδη τόξον μετὰ χερσὶν ἐνώμα,
θάλπων ἔνθα καὶ ἔνθα σέλᾳ πυρός·
sentences.l:
And Eurymachus by now the bow in his hands was handling,
warming it this way and that by the blaze of fire;
sentences.i: Meanwhile Eurymachus was already handling the bow in his hands, warming it this way and that in the blaze of the fire;
sentences.n: ἐνώμα is the imperfect of νωμάω ‘handle, turn over’, and μετὰ χερσίν is ‘in his hands’, μετά with the dative meaning ‘amid’. θάλπων is ‘warming’ and ἔνθα καὶ ἔνθα ‘this way and that’. σέλᾳ is the dative of σέλας ‘blaze, gleam’, ‘by the glow’. ἤδη means ‘by now, already’. The bow is turned in the heat while Eurymachus tries to string it.

sentences.t:
ἀλλά μιν οὐδ’ ὣς
ἐντανύσαι δύνατο, μέγα δ’ ἔστενε κυδάλιμον κῆρ·
sentences.l:
but it not even so
to string could he, and greatly he groaned in his glorious heart;
sentences.i: but even so he could not string it, and he groaned deeply in his glorious heart;
sentences.n: μιν is ‘it’, the bow, the object of ἐντανύσαι ‘to string’. οὐδ’ ὥς is ‘not even so’, with accented ὥς ‘thus’. δύνατο is the imperfect of δύναμαι without augment (Attic ἐδύνατο). ἔστενε ‘groaned’ is the imperfect of στένω, with μέγα as an adverb. κυδάλιμος ‘glorious’ is a stock epithet, translated every time; κῆρ is ‘heart’.

sentences.t: ὀχθήσας δ’ ἄρα εἶπεν ἔπος τ’ ἔφατ’ ἔκ τ’ ὀνόμαζεν·
sentences.l: And, vexed, he then said, and spoke a word, and called them by name:
sentences.i: Troubled, he spoke, calling them by name:
sentences.n: ὀχθήσας is the aorist participle of ὀχθέω ‘be vexed, troubled’. εἶπεν ἔπος τ’ ἔφατ’ ἔκ τ’ ὀνόμαζεν is a speech-opening formula, ἔφατ’ being ἔφατο, with ἔκ … ὀνόμαζεν a verb whose preverb stands apart. It need not mean that a name is used: Eurymachus addresses the suitors as a body, and no name occurs in his speech.

sentences.t: ὢ πόποι, ἦ μοι ἄχος περί τ’ αὐτοῦ καὶ περὶ πάντων·
sentences.l: “Ah! truly to me there is grief, both about myself and about all;
sentences.i: “Ah, I feel grief, both for myself and for all of us;
sentences.n: ὢ πόποι is an exclamation of dismay, ‘Ah!’. ἦ μοι ἄχος has no verb: ‘truly to me (there is) grief’. αὐτοῦ is the genitive of αὐτός ‘self’, read here as ‘myself’, and περὶ … καὶ περί ‘about … and about’ takes the genitive of the grief’s cause. πάντων ‘all’ takes in the other suitors.

sentences.t: οὔ τι γάμου τοσσοῦτον ὀδύρομαι, ἀχνύμενός περ·
sentences.l: Not at all so much for the marriage do I lament, grieved though I am;
sentences.i: It is not so much the marriage that I lament, grieved though I am;
sentences.n: οὔ τι … τοσσοῦτον is ‘not so very much’: τι ‘at all’ weakens the denial, and τοσσοῦτον, with double σ, is the adverb ‘so much’. γάμου is a genitive of cause, ‘for the marriage’, with ὀδύρομαι ‘lament’. ἀχνύμενός περ is ‘though grieved’, περ with a participle giving concession, where Attic uses καίπερ.

sentences.t:
εἰσὶ καὶ ἄλλαι πολλαὶ Ἀχαιΐδες, αἱ μὲν ἐν αὐτῇ
ἀμφιάλῳ Ἰθάκῃ, αἱ δ’ ἄλλῃσιν πολίεσσιν·
sentences.l:
There are also many other Achaean women, some in
sea-girt Ithaca itself, and others in other cities;
sentences.i: There are many other Achaean women too, some in sea-girt Ithaca itself, others in other cities;
sentences.n: Ἀχαιΐδες is ‘Achaean women’, the feminine plural of an adjective used as a noun. αἱ μὲν … αἱ δέ is ‘some … others’, the article being a pronoun. ἐν αὐτῇ … Ἰθάκῃ is ‘in Ithaca itself’, and ἀμφιάλῳ ‘sea-girt’ is the stock epithet, translated every time. ἄλλῃσιν πολίεσσιν is a dative plural in -ῃσιν and -εσσιν, ‘in other cities’.

sentences.t:
ἀλλ’ εἰ δὴ τοσσόνδε βίης ἐπιδευέες εἰμὲν
ἀντιθέου Ὀδυσῆος, ὅ τ’ οὐ δυνάμεσθα τανύσσαι
τόξον·
sentences.i: But if we really are so far short of godlike Odysseus in strength, that we cannot string the bow;
sentences.n: ἐπιδευέες is the plural of ἐπιδευής ‘lacking’, with the genitive βίης (‘in strength’) and then ἀντιθέου Ὀδυσῆος, whose strength is the measure: ‘lacking the strength of godlike Odysseus’. εἰμέν is the epic ‘we are’. ὅ τ’ is the neuter ὅ used as a conjunction, ‘in that’. τανύσσαι is the aorist infinitive of τανύω ‘stretch’, used for stringing a bow. ἀντίθεος ‘godlike’ is translated every time.

sentences.t: ἐλεγχείη δὲ καὶ ἐσσομένοισι πυθέσθαι.
sentences.l: but a disgrace, even for those yet to be, to hear of.”
sentences.i: it is a disgrace even for those yet to come to hear of.”
sentences.n: ἐλεγχείη ‘disgrace, reproach’ has no verb, ‘(it is) a disgrace’, and the infinitive πυθέσθαι ‘to learn, to hear of’ says what is disgraceful. ἐσσομένοισι is the dative plural participle of εἰμί in its epic form, ‘for those who will be’, with καί ‘even’. This ends Eurymachus’ speech.

sentences.t: τὸν δ’ αὖτ’ Ἀντίνοος προσέφη, Εὐπείθεος υἱός·
sentences.l: Him then in turn addressed Antinous, Eupeithes’ son:
sentences.i: Then Antinous, son of Eupeithes, spoke to him in turn:
sentences.n: τὸν δ’ αὖτ’ … προσέφη is the reply-formula, ‘him then in turn addressed’: τόν is ‘him’, αὖτε ‘in turn’, and προσέφη the aorist of πρόσφημι ‘speak to’. Εὐπείθεος υἱός ‘son of Eupeithes’ is the patronymic, with the genitive in -εος (Attic -ους).

sentences.t: Εὐρύμαχ’, οὐχ οὕτως ἔσται·
sentences.l: “Eurymachus, not so will it be;
sentences.i: “Eurymachus, it will not be so;
sentences.n: οὐχ οὕτως ἔσται is ‘it will not be so’, a flat rejection of what Eurymachus has said. ἔσται is the future of εἰμί, and οὐκ becomes οὐχ before the rough breathing of οὕτως. The vocative Εὐρύμαχ’ is elided.

sentences.t: νοέεις δὲ καὶ αὐτός.
sentences.l: for you perceive it also yourself.
sentences.i: You see that yourself.
sentences.n: νοέεις is the uncontracted form of νοεῖς ‘you perceive, understand’, with its object left out. καὶ αὐτός is ‘you yourself too’: Antinous says that Eurymachus knows the reason without being told, and the next line gives it.

sentences.t:
νῦν μὲν γὰρ κατὰ δῆμον ἑορτὴ τοῖο θεοῖο
ἁγνή·
sentences.l:
For now throughout the land there is a festival of the god,
pure;
sentences.i: For today there is a festival of the god throughout the land, a pure one;
sentences.n: κατὰ δῆμον is ‘throughout the land’, δῆμος being kept as ‘land’. τοῖο θεοῖο is ‘of that god’: τοῖο is the genitive of the article-pronoun in -οιο (Attic τοῦ), and the god is named as Apollo at line 267. ἁγνή ‘pure’ goes with ἑορτή ‘festival’ and means ritually clean and hallowed. νῦν μὲν γάρ gives the reason, ‘for now’.

sentences.t: τίς δέ κε τόξα τιταίνοιτ’;
sentences.l: and who would stretch bows?
sentences.i: who, then, would bend a bow?
sentences.n: τίς δέ κε … τιταίνοιτ’ is a question with κε and the optative, ‘who would stretch …?’, to which the answer is that nobody would. τιταίνω ‘stretch, strain’ is used for working a bow. τόξα is a plural that can stand for a single bow; it returns in line 264.

sentences.t:
ἀλλὰ ἕκηλοι
κάτθετ’·
sentences.l:
but at ease
lay them down;
sentences.i: No, lay them down and be at ease;
sentences.n: κάτθετ’ is κάτθετε, the aorist imperative plural of κατατίθημι ‘put down’, with the preverb joined to the verb and the τ doubled. ἕκηλοι ‘at ease, undisturbed’ is a plural predicate, ‘in peace’. ἀλλά here is ‘no, but’, turning from the question to the advice.

sentences.t:
ἀτὰρ πελέκεάς γε καὶ εἴ κ’ εἰῶμεν ἅπαντας
ἑστάμεν·
sentences.l:
but the axes, at least, even if we let them all
stand;
sentences.i: as for the axes, even if we leave them all standing;
sentences.n: ἀτάρ is ‘but, and’, and γε stresses πελέκεάς, the accusative plural of πέλεκυς ‘axe’ in the open form -εας (Attic πελέκεις). καὶ εἴ κ’ is ‘even if’, with εἰῶμεν the short-vowel subjunctive of ἐάω ‘let, allow’. ἑστάμεν is the perfect infinitive of ἵστημι, ‘to stand’ (Attic ἑστάναι). ἅπαντας ‘all’ agrees with the axes, the row set up for the contest.

sentences.t:
οὐ μὲν γάρ τιν’ ἀναιρήσεσθαι ὀΐω,
ἐλθόντ’ ἐς μέγαρον Λαερτιάδεω Ὀδυσῆος.
sentences.l:
for no one, I think, will take them up,
having come into the hall of Odysseus son of Laertes.
sentences.i: for I do not think anyone will carry them off, coming into the hall of Odysseus, son of Laertes.
sentences.n: οὐ μὲν γάρ is ‘for surely not’. ἀναιρήσεσθαι is the future middle infinitive of ἀναιρέω ‘take up, carry off’, after ὀΐω ‘I think’; the accusative τιν’ ‘anyone’ is its subject, and ἐλθόντ’ agrees with it. In English the ‘not’ goes with ‘think’. Λαερτιάδεω is the genitive of Λαερτιάδης ‘son of Laertes’, with -εω for -ου.

sentences.t:
ἀλλ’ ἄγετ’, οἰνοχόος μὲν ἐπαρξάσθω δεπάεσσιν,
ὄφρα σπείσαντες καταθείομεν ἀγκύλα τόξα·
sentences.l:
But come, let the wine-pourer pour the first drops into the cups,
so that, having poured libations, we may lay down the curved bows;
sentences.i: But come, let the cupbearer first pour a few drops into each cup, so that after our libations we may lay the curved bows aside;
sentences.n: ἐπαρξάσθω is the aorist imperative, third person, of ἐπάρχομαι ‘pour the first drops’, the opening of the round of cups; οἰνοχόος is ‘wine-pourer’. The first line repeats one already shipped. καταθείομεν is a short-vowel aorist subjunctive in -είομεν, ‘we may lay down’, after ὄφρα. ἀγκύλα ‘curved’ qualifies τόξα, a plural for one bow or several.

sentences.t:
ἠῶθεν δὲ κέλεσθε Μελάνθιον, αἰπόλον αἰγῶν,
αἶγας ἄγειν, αἳ πᾶσι μέγ’ ἔξοχοι αἰπολίοισιν,
ὄφρ’ ἐπὶ μηρία θέντες Ἀπόλλωνι κλυτοτόξῳ
τόξου πειρώμεσθα καὶ ἐκτελέωμεν ἄεθλον.
sentences.l:
and at dawn urge Melanthius, the goatherd of goats,
to bring goats, which stand out greatly among all herds of goats,
so that, having laid on thigh-pieces for Apollo famous-bowed, we
may make trial of the bow and bring to an end the contest.”
sentences.i: and at dawn tell Melanthius, the goatherd of the goats, to bring goats, those that stand out above all the herds, so that, after laying thigh-pieces on for Apollo of the famous bow, we may try the bow and bring the contest to its end.”
sentences.n: κέλεσθε is the plural imperative of κέλομαι ‘urge, tell’, with the infinitive ἄγειν ‘to bring’. ἠῶθεν is ‘at dawn’. αἳ … μέγ’ ἔξοχοι is ‘which stand out greatly’, with αἰπολίοισιν ‘herds of goats’. ἐπὶ … θέντες is tmesis, ‘laying on’ (the altar understood) μηρία, the thigh-pieces burnt for the gods. Ἀπόλλωνι κλυτοτόξῳ is ‘to Apollo of the famous bow’. The last line repeats one already shipped.

sentences.t: ὣς ἔφατ’ Ἀντίνοος, τοῖσιν δ’ ἐπιήνδανε μῦθος.
sentences.l: So spoke Antinous, and to them the word was pleasing.
sentences.i: So spoke Antinous, and his words pleased them.
sentences.n: ὣς ἔφατ’ closes a speech: ἔφατ’ is ἔφατο, the imperfect middle of φημί. τοῖσιν is ‘to them’, a dative of the persons pleased, and ἐπιήνδανε is the imperfect of ἐπιανδάνω ‘please’. μῦθος is ‘word, speech’.

sentences.t:
τοῖσι δὲ κήρυκες μὲν ὕδωρ ἐπὶ χεῖρας ἔχευαν,
κοῦροι δὲ κρητῆρας ἐπεστέψαντο ποτοῖο,
νώμησαν δ’ ἄρα πᾶσιν ἐπαρξάμενοι δεπάεσσιν.
sentences.l:
and for them the heralds poured water over their hands,
and young men filled the mixing-bowls to the brim with drink,
and they dealt it out to all, having first poured drops into the cups.
sentences.i: and the heralds poured water over their hands, young men filled the mixing-bowls to the brim with drink, and they served it out to all, first pouring a few drops into each cup.
sentences.n: τοῖσι is ‘for them’, a dative of interest, and three clauses with δέ list the tasks of the heralds, the young men and then ‘they’. ἐπεστέψαντο is the aorist middle of ἐπιστέφομαι ‘fill to the brim’, literally ‘crown’. νώμησαν is from νωμάω ‘deal out’ (‘handle’ at line 245), and ἐπαρξάμενοι from ἐπάρχομαι ‘pour the first drops’. The first two lines, and the third in an earlier book, repeat shipped lines.

sentences.t:
οἱ δ’ ἐπεὶ οὖν σπεῖσάν τ’ ἔπιόν θ’ ὅσον ἤθελε θυμός,
τοῖς δὲ δολοφρονέων μετέφη πολύμητις Ὀδυσσεύς·
sentences.l:
And they, when then they had poured libations and drunk as much as the heart wished,
among them, with guile in his mind, spoke many-wiled Odysseus:
sentences.i: When they had poured their libations and drunk as much as their hearts wished, Odysseus of many wiles, with guile in his mind, spoke among them:
sentences.n: οἱ δ’ ἐπεὶ οὖν is ‘and they, when then’. σπεῖσάν is ἔσπεισαν ‘poured libations’ and ἔπιον ‘drank’, both without augment. ὅσον ἤθελε θυμός, ‘as much as the heart wished’, is the stock phrase for drinking one’s fill. The second line is a whole line already shipped: δολοφρονέων ‘with guile in his mind’, μετέφη ‘spoke among’, πολύμητις ‘many-wiled’; the δέ after τοῖς is left to the sentence.

sentences.t: κέκλυτέ μευ, μνηστῆρες ἀγακλειτῆς βασιλείης·
sentences.l: “Hear me, suitors of the renowned queen;
sentences.i: “Hear me, suitors of the renowned queen;
sentences.n: κέκλυτε is an imperative of the perfect type of κλύω, with present force, and μευ is the genitive of ἐγώ (Attic μου) after a verb of hearing. βασιλείης is the Ionic genitive of βασίλεια ‘queen’; Penelope is meant, but not named. ἀγακλειτῆς ‘renowned’ is translated every time.

sentences.t: ὄφρ’ εἴπω τά με θυμὸς ἐνὶ στήθεσσι κελεύει·
sentences.l: that I may say what my heart in my breast bids;
sentences.i: so that I may say what the heart in my breast bids me say;
sentences.n: ὄφρ’ εἴπω is ‘so that I may say’, ὄφρα with the aorist subjunctive for purpose. τά με θυμὸς … κελεύει is ‘what my heart bids’: τά is the relative ‘what’, and με the object. ἐνὶ στήθεσσιν is ‘in the breast’, plural for singular, with the dative ending -εσσιν. The whole line is one already shipped.

sentences.t:
Εὐρύμαχον δὲ μάλιστα καὶ Ἀντίνοον θεοειδέα
λίσσομ’, ἐπεὶ καὶ τοῦτο ἔπος κατὰ μοῖραν ἔειπε,
νῦν μὲν παῦσαι τόξον, ἐπιτρέψαι δὲ θεοῖσιν·
sentences.i: And I beg Eurymachus above all, and Antinous, godlike in form, since he has spoken this word too as is fitting: for now let the bow rest, and entrust it to the gods;
sentences.n: λίσσομ’ is λίσσομαι ‘I beg’, with two accusative objects and two infinitives for what is begged. παῦσαι read as an infinitive is ‘make rest’, ‘let the bow rest’ (it could also be an imperative ‘stop with the bow’), and ἐπιτρέψαι δὲ θεοῖσιν is ‘entrust it to the gods’. ἔειπε is the aorist of εἶπον with its old double ε-. Its singular subject is not named, and presumably is Antinous, who spoke last. κατὰ μοῖραν is ‘as is fitting’. θεοειδέα ‘godlike in form’ is translated every time.

sentences.t: ἠῶθεν δὲ θεὸς δώσει κράτος ᾧ κ’ ἐθέλῃσιν.
sentences.l: and at dawn a god will give power to whom he wishes.
sentences.i: and at dawn a god will give power to whomever he wishes.
sentences.n: ἠῶθεν δέ ‘and at dawn’ answers the νῦν μὲν of the line before. κράτος is ‘power, mastery’, here the success that a god grants. θεός is ‘a god’, left unnamed. ᾧ κ’ ἐθέλῃσιν is an indefinite relative with κε and the subjunctive, ‘to whom he may wish’.

sentences.t:
ἀλλ’ ἄγ’ ἐμοὶ δότε τόξον ἐΰξοον, ὄφρα μεθ’ ὑμῖν
χειρῶν καὶ σθένεος πειρήσομαι, ἤ μοι ἔτ’ ἐστὶν
ἴς, οἵη πάρος ἔσκεν ἐνὶ γναμπτοῖσι μέλεσσιν,
ἦ ἤδη μοι ὄλεσσεν ἄλη τ’ ἀκομιστίη τε.
sentences.l:
But come, give me the well-polished bow, that among you
of my hands and strength I may make trial, whether I have still
force, such as it was before in my pliant limbs,
or whether already it has destroyed for me wandering and lack of tending.”
sentences.i: But come, give me the well-polished bow, so that among you I may try my hands and my strength, to see whether I still have the force I once had in my pliant limbs, or whether wandering and lack of care have already destroyed it.”
sentences.n: ἐΰξοον is ‘well-polished’. πειρήσομαι takes the genitives χειρῶν καὶ σθένεος ‘of hands and strength’: he will try them against the bow. ἤ … ἦ is ‘whether … or whether’. ἔσκεν is an old past of εἰμί, ‘used to be’. ἴς is ‘force’, γναμπτοῖσι μέλεσσιν ‘pliant limbs’, with datives in -οισι and -εσσιν. ὄλεσσεν, the aorist of ὄλλυμι, has two subjects, ἄλη ‘wandering’ and ἀκομιστίη, a rare noun ‘lack of tending’.

sentences.t:
ὣς ἔφαθ’, οἱ δ’ ἄρα πάντες ὑπερφιάλως νεμέσησαν,
δείσαντες μὴ τόξον ἐΰξοον ἐντανύσειεν.
sentences.l:
So he spoke, and they all then beyond measure were indignant,
fearing lest he string the well-polished bow.
sentences.i: So he spoke, and all of them were indignant beyond measure, afraid that he might string the well-polished bow.
sentences.n: ὑπερφιάλως is the adverb of ὑπερφίαλος, here ‘beyond measure’, as in the same line shipped earlier, where it ended at a raised dot. νεμέσησαν is from νεμεσάω ‘be indignant’. δείσαντες is the aorist participle of δείδω ‘fear’, and μή with the optative ἐντανύσειεν gives what is feared, ‘lest he string’. The optative follows a past main verb.

sentences.t: Ἀντίνοος δ’ ἐνένιπεν ἔπος τ’ ἔφατ’ ἔκ τ’ ὀνόμαζεν·
sentences.l: And Antinous rebuked him, and spoke a word, and called him by name:
sentences.i: Antinous rebuked him, and spoke, calling him by name:
sentences.n: ἐνένιπεν is the aorist of ἐνίπτω ‘rebuke’, with the stranger as the understood object. ἔπος τ’ ἔφατ’ ἔκ τ’ ὀνόμαζεν is a stock formula for a speaker’s address, ἔκ … ὀνόμαζεν a verb with its preverb standing apart. It need not mean that a name is used, and Antinous’s first word for him is δειλὲ ξείνων.

sentences.t: ἆ δειλὲ ξείνων, ἔνι τοι φρένες οὐδ’ ἠβαιαί·
sentences.l: “Ah, miserable among strangers, in you there are not even slight wits;
sentences.i: “Ah, miserable stranger, you have not even a little sense in you;
sentences.n: ἆ is an exclamation of scorn, and δειλὲ ξείνων is ‘miserable among strangers’, a partitive genitive; δειλός is ‘wretched’, here with contempt. ἔνι is ἔνεστι ‘is in’, with the accent drawn back, and τοι is σοι ‘in you’. φρένες are ‘wits’, and οὐδ’ ἠβαιαί ‘not even slight’ ends the line.

sentences.l:
Are you not content that at ease among us overweening men
you feast, and are in no way deprived of the feast, but also hear
our words and our talk?
sentences.i: Are you not content to feast at ease among us overweening men, deprived of no share of the feast, and to hear our words and our talk?
sentences.n: οὐκ ἀγαπᾷς ὅ is ‘are you not content that’, with ὅ as a conjunction. ἕκηλος is ‘at ease’. ὑπερφιάλοισι μεθ’ ἡμῖν is ‘among us overweening men’: ὑπερφίαλος is usually a reproach, and Antinous applies it to his own company, perhaps with pride. δαίνυσαι is ‘you feast’, and ἀμέρδεαι is the middle of ἀμέρδω ‘deprive’, ‘you are deprived’, with the genitive δαιτός. ῥήσιος is from ῥῆσις ‘speech’.

sentences.t:
οὐδέ τις ἄλλος
ἡμετέρων μύθων ξεῖνος καὶ πτωχὸς ἀκούει.
sentences.l:
and not any other
of our words, stranger and beggar, hears.
sentences.i: No other stranger or beggar hears our words.
sentences.n: ἀκούει takes the genitive ἡμετέρων μύθων, ‘hears our words’. οὐδέ τις ἄλλος … ξεῖνος καὶ πτωχός is ‘nor any other stranger and beggar’. ἡμετέρων ‘our’ was the last word of the line before as well: Antinous says ‘our’ twice in two lines, marking the talk as the suitors’ own.

sentences.t:
οἶνός σε τρώει μελιηδής, ὅς τε καὶ ἄλλους
βλάπτει, ὃς ἄν μιν χανδὸν ἕλῃ μηδ’ αἴσιμα πίνῃ.
sentences.l:
Honey-sweet wine wounds you, which also others
harms, whoever takes it greedily and does not drink in due measure.
sentences.i: Honey-sweet wine is hurting you, wine that harms others too, whoever takes it greedily and does not drink in due measure.
sentences.n: τρώει is ‘wounds, harms’, from τρώω. ὅς τε is ‘which’, with the epic τε of a general truth, and καὶ ἄλλους ‘others too’. ὃς ἄν … ἕλῃ is ‘whoever takes’, with ἄν and the subjunctive, and μιν is ‘it’, the wine. χανδόν is an adverb related to χάσκω ‘gape’, so ‘greedily’; its exact sense is not certain. αἴσιμα ‘in due measure’, from αἶσα ‘portion’, is a neuter plural used as an adverb.

sentences.t:
οἶνος καὶ Κένταυρον, ἀγακλυτὸν Εὐρυτίωνα,
ἄασ’ ἐνὶ μεγάρῳ μεγαθύμου Πειριθόοιο,
ἐς Λαπίθας ἐλθόνθ’·
sentences.i: Wine also bewildered the Centaur Eurytion, the renowned, in the hall of great-hearted Peirithous, when he had come to the Lapiths;
sentences.n: ἄασ’ is ἄασε, the aorist of ἀάω ‘bewilder, cloud the mind of’. The word and its relatives (ἄασεν, ἀασθείς, ἄτην) run through this story, and the translation keeps them as ‘bewilder’ and ‘bewilderment’. Κένταυρον and Εὐρυτίωνα are accusatives, ἀγακλυτός ‘renowned’ the epithet, and μεγαθύμου ‘great-hearted’ goes with Πειριθόοιο. ἐλθόνθ’ is the accusative participle, elided, agreeing with Κένταυρον.

sentences.t:
ὁ δ’ ἐπεὶ φρένας ἄασεν οἴνῳ,
μαινόμενος κάκ’ ἔρεξε δόμον κάτα Πειριθόοιο·
sentences.l:
and he, when he had bewildered his wits with wine,
raging, did evil things throughout the house of Peirithous;
sentences.i: and when he had bewildered his wits with wine, he raged and did evil throughout the house of Peirithous;
sentences.n: ἄασεν is again ἀάω, now with φρένας ‘wits’ as its object and οἴνῳ ‘with wine’ as the means: the man has bewildered his own wits. μαινόμενος ‘raging’ is the participle of μαίνομαι. κάκ’ is κακά elided, and ἔρεξε the aorist of ῥέζω ‘do’. δόμον κάτα is κατὰ δόμον with the preposition after its noun and its accent drawn back, ‘throughout the house’.

sentences.t:
ἥρωας δ’ ἄχος εἷλε, διὲκ προθύρου δὲ θύραζε
ἕλκον ἀναΐξαντες, ἀπ’ οὔατα νηλέϊ χαλκῷ
ῥῖνάς τ’ ἀμήσαντες·
sentences.i: Grief seized the heroes, and they sprang up and dragged him out through the forecourt and out of doors, cutting off his ears and nose with pitiless bronze;
sentences.n: ἥρωας is the accusative plural of ἥρως ‘hero’, here the Lapith nobles; ἄχος εἷλε is ‘grief seized’. διὲκ προθύρου δὲ θύραζε is ‘out through the forecourt, out of doors’, with θύραζε in the direction-suffix -ζε. ἕλκον is ‘dragged’, ἀναΐξαντες ‘springing up’. ἀπ’ … ἀμήσαντες is tmesis, ‘cutting off’, with οὔατα ‘ears’ and ῥῖνάς, a plural meaning ‘nostrils’, put as English ‘nose’. νηλέϊ ‘pitiless’ goes with χαλκῷ ‘bronze’.

sentences.t:
ὁ δὲ φρεσὶν ᾗσιν ἀασθεὶς
ἤϊεν ἣν ἄτην ὀχέων ἀεσίφρονι θυμῷ.
sentences.l:
and he, in his own wits bewildered,
went off bearing his own bewilderment with a senseless heart.
sentences.i: and he, with his wits bewildered, went his way carrying his own bewilderment in a senseless heart.
sentences.n: ᾗσιν and ἣν are both the possessive ὅς, ἥ, ὅν ‘his own’, not the relative: φρεσὶν ᾗσιν is ‘in his own wits’, and ἣν ἄτην ‘his own bewilderment’. ἀασθείς is the passive aorist participle of ἀάω. ἄτη is the state of clouded mind and the ruin it brings. ἤϊεν is the imperfect of εἶμι ‘go’, ὀχέων the participle of ὀχέω ‘carry’. ἀεσίφρονι is a rare compound whose meaning is not known for certain; ‘senseless’ is the traditional guess.

sentences.t:
ἐξ οὗ Κενταύροισι καὶ ἀνδράσι νεῖκος ἐτύχθη,
οἷ δ’ αὐτῷ πρώτῳ κακὸν εὕρετο οἰνοβαρείων.
sentences.l:
From which time, for Centaurs and men, strife was made,
but for himself first he found evil, heavy with wine.
sentences.i: From that time strife arose between the Centaurs and men; but it was he himself who first found evil, weighed down with wine.
sentences.n: ἐξ οὗ is ‘from which time’, joining the strife to the events just told. Κενταύροισι and ἀνδράσι are datives, ‘for the Centaurs and men’, and νεῖκος ἐτύχθη is ‘strife was made’, the passive aorist of τεύχω. οἷ is the dative of the reflexive pronoun, ‘for himself’, and αὐτῷ πρώτῳ strengthens it. εὕρετο is the aorist middle of εὑρίσκω ‘find for oneself’, and οἰνοβαρείων the participle of οἰνοβαρέω ‘be heavy with wine’, a rare verb.

sentences.t:
ὣς καὶ σοὶ μέγα πῆμα πιφαύσκομαι, αἴ κε τὸ τόξον
ἐντανύσῃς·
sentences.l:
So also to you great woe I proclaim, if the bow
you string;
sentences.i: So too I proclaim great woe for you, if you string the bow;
sentences.n: ὣς καὶ σοί is ‘so also for you’, drawing the lesson of the story. πιφαύσκομαι is ‘I make known, proclaim’, and here is a threat, with μέγα πῆμα ‘great woe’. αἴ κε with the aorist subjunctive ἐντανύσῃς is a condition that looks forward, αἰ being the epic form of εἰ. τὸ τόξον with the article is ‘the bow’ in question.

sentences.t:
οὐ γάρ τευ ἐπητύος ἀντιβολήσεις
ἡμετέρῳ ἐνὶ δήμῳ, ἄφαρ δέ σε νηῒ μελαίνῃ
εἰς Ἔχετον βασιλῆα, βροτῶν δηλήμονα πάντων,
πέμψομεν·
sentences.l:
for of no courtesy will you meet with
in our land, and at once you in a black ship
to Echetus the king, bane of all mortals,
we will send;
sentences.i: for you will meet with no courtesy in our land, and at once we will send you in a black ship to King Echetus, the bane of all mortals;
sentences.n: οὐ γάρ τευ ἐπητύος ἀντιβολήσεις: τευ is τινός ‘any’, the genitive after ἀντιβολέω ‘meet with, partake of’. ἐπητύς is a rare noun, ‘courtesy’ by the usual guess, its derivation not certain. ἡμετέρῳ ἐνὶ δήμῳ is ‘in our land’, with ἐνί set between adjective and noun. ἄφαρ is ‘at once’, and πέμψομεν the future ‘we will send’. The line naming Echetus repeats one already shipped.

sentences.t: ἔνθεν δ’ οὔ τι σαώσεαι·
sentences.l: and from there not at all will you be saved;
sentences.i: and from there you will not be saved at all;
sentences.n: ἔνθεν is ‘from there’, with the suffix -θεν of origin, and οὔ τι ‘not at all’. σαώσεαι is the future of σαόω (the verb behind σώζω ‘save’) in a middle or passive form, ‘you will be saved’, with the uncontracted ending -εαι (Attic -ῃ). ‘There’ is the land of Echetus named in the line before.

sentences.t:
ἀλλὰ ἕκηλος
πῖνέ τε, μηδ’ ἐρίδαινε μετ’ ἀνδράσι κουροτέροισιν.
sentences.l:
but at ease
drink, and do not strive among younger men.”
sentences.i: But drink at your ease, and do not compete with younger men.”
sentences.n: πῖνε and ἐρίδαινε are imperatives, the second negated by μηδ’ ‘and do not’; ἐρίδαινε is from ἐριδαίνω ‘quarrel, contend’, a verb built on ἔρις ‘strife’. μετ’ ἀνδράσι κουροτέροισιν is ‘among younger men’, κουρότερος being the comparative of κοῦρος ‘youth’, and μετά with the dative ‘among’. ἕκηλος ‘at ease’ is singular here. This ends Antinous’ speech.

sentences.t: τὸν δ’ αὖτε προσέειπε περίφρων Πηνελόπεια·
sentences.l: Him then in turn addressed circumspect Penelope:
sentences.i: Then circumspect Penelope spoke to him in turn:
sentences.n: τὸν δ’ αὖτε προσέειπε is the reply-formula, ‘him then in turn addressed’, with προσέειπε the aorist of προσεῖπον ‘speak to’ in its epic form. περίφρων ‘circumspect’ is the epithet of Penelope, from περί ‘around’ and φρήν ‘mind’, and is translated every time.

sentences.t:
Ἀντίνο’, οὐ μὲν καλὸν ἀτέμβειν οὐδὲ δίκαιον
ξείνους Τηλεμάχου, ὅς κεν τάδε δώμαθ’ ἵκηται·
sentences.l:
“Antinous, it is not indeed fine to cheat, nor just,
Telemachus’ strangers, whoever may come to this house;
sentences.i: “Antinous, it is neither fine nor just to cheat Telemachus’ strangers, whoever may come to this house;
sentences.n: οὐ μὲν καλὸν … οὐδὲ δίκαιον is ‘it is not indeed fine, nor just’. ἀτέμβειν is a rare infinitive; its sense, ‘cheat, wrong’, comes from the context and is not securely known. ξείνους Τηλεμάχου is ‘Telemachus’ strangers’, plural, and the relative clause turns to the singular, ὅς κεν … ἵκηται ‘whoever may come’, with κεν and the subjunctive. δώμαθ’ is δώματα, a plural for one house. The second line is one already shipped.

sentences.l:
Do you expect, if the stranger the great bow of Odysseus
strings, trusting both in his hands and in his own strength,
to take me home and make me his own wife?
sentences.i: Do you expect that if the stranger strings the great bow of Odysseus, trusting in his hands and his own strength, he will take me home and make me his own wife?
sentences.n: ἔλπεαι is ‘you expect’, the second person of ἔλπομαι, uncontracted. It takes the future infinitives ἄξεσθαι and θήσεσθαι with ‘he’ understood, and αἴ χ’ … ἐντανύσῃ is the condition inside. βίηφι has the old ending -φι, ‘by force’, and ἧφι is the possessive ὅς with the same ending, ‘his own’; ἑήν is the possessive again. πιθήσας is from πείθομαι ‘trust’ and takes the dative. ἄκοιτιν is ‘wife’.

sentences.t: οὐδ’ αὐτός που τοῦτό γ’ ἐνὶ στήθεσσιν ἔολπε·
sentences.l: Nor does he himself, I suppose, hope this at least in his breast;
sentences.i: Nor, I suppose, does he himself hope for this in his breast;
sentences.n: οὐδ’ αὐτός is ‘nor … himself’: Penelope says the stranger does not himself hope for what Antinous fears. που ‘I suppose’ softens the claim. ἔολπε, from ἔλπω, is a perfect-type form with present sense, ‘hopes’; the reduplication ἐ- is old. τοῦτό γ’ ‘this at least’ is its object, and στήθεσσιν is a dative plural in -εσσιν.

sentences.t:
μηδέ τις ὑμείων τοῦ γ’ εἵνεκα θυμὸν ἀχεύων
ἐνθάδε δαινύσθω, ἐπεὶ οὐδὲ μὲν οὐδὲ ἔοικεν.
sentences.l:
Nor let any of you, for this at least, grieving in his heart,
feast here, since indeed it is not at all fitting.”
sentences.i: And let none of you feast here grieving in his heart on this account, since it is not fitting at all.”
sentences.n: μηδέ … δαινύσθω is a third-person imperative with μή, ‘let none … feast’; ὑμείων is the Ionic genitive plural of ὑμεῖς ‘of you’. τοῦ γ’ εἵνεκα is ‘on this account’, εἵνεκα being ἕνεκα, and θυμὸν ἀχεύων is ‘grieving in his heart’, an accusative of respect. ἐπεὶ οὐδὲ μὲν οὐδὲ ἔοικεν piles up negatives, ‘since indeed it is not at all fitting’; ἔοικεν is a perfect with present sense. This ends Penelope’s speech and the part.
